90.t: Arriving at Club Alabam and the Downbeat on Central Avenue
90.s: First night on Central Avenue and the layout of the Downbeat, his all-time favorite club.
90.ch: Wartime South and the Ernie Fields band
90.q: We went into Lincoln, Nebraska to play...and the next stop was Los Angeles (hah-hah-hah!) at the Club Alabam on Central Avenue between 42nd and 42nd Place. And I never will forget it. We got in in the middle of...oh, somewhere about 11:30 or 12 o'clock. And Central Avenue was just full of people.…

90.s: Casablanca, Cafe Society, Big Jim Wynn, and other late places on San Pedro, with Red Mack and Tom Archia.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: And then they had plenty of after-hour places, like the Casablanca over on San Pedro. After-hours was anything that was open after two o'clock, because as it is now in California, at two o'clock all the legal things shut down, you know, unless you have some kind of charter for a private club or…

90.t: Gerald Wilson's band and Central Avenue after-hours
90.s: Gerald Wilson's band with Melba Liston at Shepp's and the after-hours places on Central.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: had Jimmy Bunn playing piano and writing for the band, and Hobart Dotson, one of fine trumpet players, and Tucker Green was playing drums, and... He had a fine band. Melba Liston was with the band. She was writing and playing her trombone with the band. That's where I first met all of that gang,…

90.t: Jack's Basket Room and Wild Bill Moore as impresario
90.s: After-hours at Jack's Basket Room where Wild Bill Moore handled the hiring.
90.ch: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
90.q: We'd go from place to place and play all around at the after-hour spots. Jack's Basket was up on Central and 27th, or 29th, something like that. It was very popular. It was a bigger place. And during this time, Wild Bill Moore had moved out here, and he was kind of like the impresario at Jack's…

90.s: His father's letter warned him to leave California; back in LA the clubs had closed, and he met Al Hibbler and Al Killian.
90.ch: San Francisco and the postwar slump
90.q: : This was February of '46. I'll never forget, my father wrote me a letter. He said, "Look, the war is winding down. Get out of California." He said, "Because it's no good for musicians and entertainers." He had been out here with shows years ago, you know, and he said "It's not the place to be."…

90.t: Western Avenue: the Ringside and Hi-De-Ho Club
90.s: With Central Avenue clubs closing, Western Avenue took over, including Alton Redd's Ringside and the Hi-De-Ho Club.
90.ch: San Francisco and the postwar slump
90.q: Most of the clubs on Central Avenue and the east side had folded, and things were beginning to move west music-wise. The next big music stop was Western Avenue. And it had places like the Ringside on Washington and Western. I used to play over there with Vi Redd's father, Alton Redd. He used to…

90.t: Hollywood clubs: Radio Room, Hangover and the Empire Room
90.s: Lucky Thompson at the Radio Room, Dixieland at the Hangover, and Woody Herman's Four Brothers.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: : Well, we were like the session group. And when Dexter was on, Dexter was here. And Lucky Thompson, the fine tenor saxophone player, he had migrated to California with Boyd Raeburn's big band, and they played at the Radio Room up on Vine, between Selma and Hollywood Boulevard.

90.s: Gerald Wilson's band upstairs and combos below at Shepp's, and Eddie Heywood's group's hit.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: And down around the First and San Pedro area, they had Shepp's Playhouse. Gerald Wilson's big band was upstairs, and they had smaller combos downstairs, you know.

8.t: Los Angeles work and Jelly Roll, Buddy Petit
8.s: He worked for Mike Lyman and the Plantation in Culver City, played around with Jelly Roll, and saw Buddy Petit at the Red Onion.
8.q: But we was playing at the plantation out in Culver City. He built a place out there, a beautiful place. And I went to the J's room.

8.s: He refused to go to New York with Oliver and married in California in 1927.
8.q: No, I left, you see. That's what he was going to do because he wanted to go to New York. I told him I ain't going to go to New York. I'm going to stay here. I get my shoes shined the whole year around in California.

8.t: Jazz in San Francisco when the Oliver band arrived
8.s: Asked about jazz on the coast, Garland says nobody played it and Oliver's band was the best around, at a San Francisco place.
8.q: No. Still, the Prod and them had the best band around there at the right time. That was at, uh, Leicester Mapp's place.

8.t: Oakland's Creole Cafe and playing with Jelly Roll Morton at Jump Steady
8.s: After San Francisco, the band played the Creole Cafe in Oakland and a Los Angeles dance run by Jelly Roll Morton in Watts.
8.q: To Akamacha, and then after we left the Deluxe, I mean after we left the Percola, we played the Creole, then we, uh, Jolly wanted us- The Creole where? Cafe here. On Severn and Woods, where Slim Jenkins is at.

8.t: A month in Los Angeles and back with Ory
8.s: The Oliver band stayed about a month in Los Angeles, after which Oliver went east and Garland rejoined Ory.
8.q: California about -- we come down to Los Angeles. Stayed there about a month.

8.t: The Black and Tan Orchestra in Los Angeles
8.s: Garland names the members of the Black and Tan Orchestra, the leading Los Angeles house band, which played dances and entertainments.
8.q: They had everything, you know. They had little scrap bands around there, but Black and Tan was the whole go (Unintelligible). And they had a good band.

8.t: Returning the ticket and Oliver's letter
8.s: Garland meets a friend at the station and returns Oliver's ticket instead of going; Oliver wrote an angry letter.
8.q: And so much to do the bank. And that same day, just as the man gave me the money from my car and I was out of the 60th Street to the station to get this ticket, you see. Who gets off the train? I had a train. I said, Because she was on the train. I don't know what made me stop and go look out on…

677.t: Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders and owner Frank Sebastian
677.s: He names bandmates Paul Howard and George Orendorff, and describes Sebastian, who loved lights.
677.q: Yes, there was only eight men in the band at that time, so yes we were -- in fact the -- the -- what do you call the dance -- the person had the shows -- was Carolyn Snowden -- I think she's still alive. And this group called the Quality Serenaders was the band, or Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders…

677.t: Joining Curtis Mosby at the Apex Club
677.s: He left the Cotton Club for Mosby's Apex on Central Avenue, alternating months of show in Los Angeles and San Francisco.
677.q: Well, after Louis's first trip here, then we sort of shifted the -- well, I went out of the club, and I went down with Curtis Mosby, who had the Apex Club down on Central. And I traveled with him for a few months.

677.s: Mosby was a drummer turned impresario and owner; Ivie Anderson started as an ingenue there.
677.q: He was originally the drummer. In fact, he drummed several times when he'd come over -- you know -- come up and play a few sets and things like that.

677.t: Hollywood crowds at the Apex and the Cotton Club in Culver City
677.s: Movie stars and Hearst came to the Apex; the Cotton Club had three dance floors divided by drapes and room for a thousand cars.
677.q: It was, it was. And the yard was a huge place out there in Culver City. I guess you could pack a thousand cars in that yard. And the place itself was so big that when they opened up they had a system of curtain, where the curtains are like the walls. And when they drew the drapes back you had three…

677.s: On Saturday after Easter 1932 he took the train east; Ellington had never heard him, and he did not live in California again until the 1970s.
677.q: No. No, he never -- unless he'd stayed around after his -- see, they used to invite these orchestras to do a few numbers, when they were in town, as part of the show out there. And then after that they'd go on wherever they wanted to go. But it was like guests -- guestshots.

677.t: Mosby's San Francisco Apex and returning to the Cotton Club
677.s: The San Francisco Apex was on upper floors near Chinatown; Brown went in and out between Mosby and the Cotton Club, replacing Lewis Taylor.
677.q: Well, Mosby set up two clubs, one in San Francisco, and one in Los Angeles. And this club in San Francisco was kind of on the second and third floor in a building -- it was right at the beginning of Chinatown. I more or less think it was on Bush and between -- let me see. What were those streets up…

677.s: Ivie Anderson and husband Mark Neal ran a popular food-only restaurant at Vernon and Central, which grew into a housing development.
677.ch: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
677.q: Yes. She owned it, and she had a friend that took very good care of it, was a very good shopper for meats and things like that, and it flourished, and from there

29.t: Arriving in Los Angeles at about twenty knowing no one
29.s: He came to Los Angeles around age twenty simply to play his horn, with no job and no friends, and cannot recall early musicians' names.
29.ch: Opening, arrival in Los Angeles and the Quality Four
29.q: Yes, I remember. When I got to Los Angeles, let's see, when I got to Los Angeles, Buddy, I was --

29.t: Lawrence Brown joins Howard's band for the Momart
29.s: Howard says Lawrence Brown played with him at the Momart, got a minor illness back East later, and came from Pasadena with his brother Harold.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Well, Lawrence Brown came here -- of course, he came here and the first thing he did was get sick. And he played with me.

29.t: The two locations of the Apex on Central Avenue
29.s: Mrs. Howard explains the Apex moved from 43rd to 55th Street, around 1935, and that she sang there.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Sure we do. She was there, singing in it.

29.t: The 1935 opening of the new Apex at 55th and Central
29.s: Mrs. Howard reads a California News account and ad: Curtis Moseby hosting, Sue Hoye, Patsy Hunter's revue and Buck Clayton's band.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: I believe so, I believe so. The long-awaited return of Curtis Moseby to the local amusement world came to an end last week. That's Wednesday night. When the doors of the new Apex Club at 55th and Central Avenue were swung open to a brilliant gathering of celebrities there to witness the occasion.

29.t: House bands at the Bell Tavern, Alabam and Shep's Playhouse
29.s: Patsy and Collette recall house bands at Los Angeles clubs: C. L. Burke at the Bell Tavern, Johnny Otis at the Alabam, Shep's Playhouse.
29.ch: Sue and Patsy Howard in show business
29.q: I can't think right now, but there are a lot of musicians who have played in these little different places that are well known and outstanding as of today, but I can't recall any of the names.

29.t: Sue Hoye in the 1934 Cotton Club review
29.s: Willard shows a clipping about the Sebastian Cotton Club review with Sue Hoye and Patsy Hunter; Howard tires.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Let's see, Les Hite and Frank Sebastian, Lionel Hampton, don't give you all the names of the men playing in this --

29.t: Frank Sebastian, the Green Mill and the New Cotton Club
29.s: Howard describes Sebastian as a flashy sport who kept wanting his band, and agrees the New Cotton Club was at Culver City.
29.ch: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
29.q: He was a -- I don't know what you call it, but he was a very smart aleck man, and he wore clothes, boy, I'm telling you, he just dressed up like nobody's business. And he come out there and he'd get out on the stand and put his hands on his hips and (Inaudible). A lot of the people were on there.

769.t: Trumpeters, the Tin Angel and the Hangover in San Francisco
769.s: Kid Howard and Tom Jefferson join the California trips, and the band plays the Tin Angel and Doc Dougherty's Hangover.
769.q: We had, oh what this guy's name, played trumpet with Paul Ballbrand sometime. Oh I can't think of his name right now because he only played such a short time with us.

769.t: Swapping places with Cie Frazier at the Beverly Caverns
769.s: Passing through Los Angeles, Watkins finds Cie Frazier on drums with Lewis; Frazier hands the job back and buys his ticket.
769.q: Well he was on drums, he had taken my place. So I told George, I said, well I'm going to pass through Los Angeles and I'll drop by and see y'all on my way home. So, I stopped over that night and I checked my drums in and come here to New Orleans. So I stopped at the Watkins Hotel and I went on…

769.t: Hines house-band offer and return to George Lewis, 1955
769.s: Doc wanted a house band and brought Watkins out to San Francisco in August 1955. After Earl Watkins replaced him he returned to Los Angeles and rejoined George Lewis at the Beverly Cabin.
769.q: Well, they're still holding now. You see, Doc had wanted a house band. Well, we couldn't take it over because we had, George had too many commitments that was taken to different places at the time that Doc wanted us there. Well, naturally he just gave it up and got oil, you know? And Ed had wrote…

769.t: Parisian Room, Almerocka and the Cincinnati and Ohio trips
769.s: The band plays the Parisian Room and Almerocka, gets Look magazine coverage, and is taken to Cincinnati, Ohio and Indiana; a record is made in Ohio and another in San Francisco.
769.q: The Parisian Room, yeah. Yeah, the Parisian Room. Well, we played there one Saturday night, and the Almerocka Club had warned us. So, after we got through playing there was this fellow, Eddie Kidd Wolf, former friend, a dry spider, and his partner was named Frank. He was an Italian. Well, when we…

769.t: Lawrence Marrero's illness, Beverly Caverns and Cincinnati's Sinton Hotel
769.s: Back home, the band plays house parties; Marrero falls ill in Hollywood, and the band later works weekends at the Sinton Hotel.
769.q: Yeah, so Saeed left and I had to go to the station to order my drums back. They was on the way to New Orleans when I got there the following day, so they shipped them on back to me. And I taken over and we finished playing out there about two months afterwards. And we came on back home. But things…

769.t: California club scene and travel costs
769.s: He talks about the Beverly Cabin closing, other California clubs, rail fare costs for the band and layoffs at airplane plants.
769.q: And, uh, I think Joe Darinsburg is playing at some other place that this fellow opened up. It says quite a small place. It's not as big as the Beverly cabin, but, uh, they seem to be doing pretty good. The 400 is not open. Like they said, no, I think the 400 is open with Teddy Buckner. I think…

45.t: Railroad yard job and returning home to New Orleans in 1921
45.s: With the club closed Williams takes a Southern Pacific yard job, is left stranded when a drummer friend goes to Frisco, and goes home in March 1921 to join Buddy Petit, then Sam Morgan.
45.q: And they closed him up at the same time, and they mixed dancing. But he listened at him, you know, see, he didn't get smart about him, they said. But they kept telling him not to do it, and he done it, but he just come and closed him up. He didn't have to close the place. Took his license. So after…

45.t: How Los Angeles took to Ory's New Orleans band
45.s: Audiences went wild for the New Orleans band; Williams tells of jealousy over Ory's untrained trombone playing and the band's records.
45.q: Orleans people there too at that time too you know see oh they went wild over then the black and tan band well the manager Harris Southern see imagine a band you were kind of jealous of all right you see now a lot of the trombone players musicians come there it's they couldn't understand how over…

45.t: Before Los Angeles: Buddy Petit and what became of Wade Whaley
45.s: Williams was with Buddy Petit before leaving for Los Angeles in 1919, and discusses the group that went out and Wade Whaley's whereabouts.
45.q: Before I went to Los Angeles, I think I was playing with, I think I was playing with, Buddy Petit, when I went to Los Angeles. I went to Los Angeles the year of 1919.

45.t: Going to Los Angeles in 1919 with Ory's group
45.s: Williams went west with Ory's men, stayed on after the band broke up, and recalls arriving in October in a straw hat; they played the Cadillac.
45.q: No, I went out there with O'Rell. I didn't play with nobody but O'Rell. No, I didn't play with nobody but O'Rell. After the band broke up, well they raid the nightclubs, wherever that's so much, you know, and the bands broke up. And I got a job working for the railroad, working cleaning cars for…

45.t: Dink Johnson and Ernest Johnson (Nene) in Los Angeles
45.s: Discussion of Dink Johnson and the drummer Ernest Johnson, who Williams says changed his name out West, and what they played.
45.q: No, over the lake. It wasn't good in here. No, it wasn't here, no, over the lake, because I didn't know him. First time I... Did he ever play with you out there? No, he never did play. We'd seen him play with someone else.

45.t: California bands compared with New Orleans style
45.s: Williams says the Los Angeles Black and Tan band tried to play like New Orleans bands, and recalls who went west before and after him.
45.q: That's why we taken. See, now the Black and Tan band was the best band there, you know, see. Trying to play like us, you know. But after we went there, then.

116.t: Meeting Ornette Coleman in Los Angeles
116.s: He describes Ornette's concepts and his return home to teach at Xavier Prep.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: It was great, meeting Ornette. I didn’t know what Ornette was doing. A couple of times I tried to play some things with him. He had not worked out anything that included a piano. It was only a couple of months that I was up there. But it was great, just being around on that, because he was always…

116.t: Los Angeles with Ornette: no gigs, practice rooms, Charles Lloyd
116.s: With no gigs, they practice where they can; he plays once with Charles Lloyd and Billy Higgins.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: There was no gigs. Ornette used to play at his house sometimes, and sometimes he and Blackwell would play, just the two of them. Sometimes we would go over to the union building. Whatever practice room was empty, we’d run in there and set up and practice until the next person who was scheduled to…

116.t: Disliking Los Angeles: beatniks, Lenny Bruce and club scene
116.s: He explains why L.A. did not suit him and recalls Cosmo Alley, Sammy Davis, Basie and others.
116.ch: Ornette, Los Angeles and the Marines
116.q: ’58. See, rhythm-and-blues was just beginning to come to Los Angeles. Earl Palmer, who was a great drummer, he did all of the sessions here. He went to Los Angeles. He left here and went up to L.A. I would see Earl every now and then while I was in the military. The studios had guys who were used…

116.t: Playing with Dexter Gordon at the La Chris
116.s: While in the Marines he subbed for Elmo Hope and played with Dexter Gordon.
116.q: Not a square, but a long – rectangle, from front to back. I was still in the service, but I would come in when I was off from duty. I never got to really know Elmo. I went into the La Chris looking for somewhere to sit. This was a straight shoot to the bandstand. So when I came in, Elmo saw me and…

116.s: He says he never connected with L.A., and they mention Gerald Wilson and Snooky Young.
116.q: Los Angeles was an interesting place at that time, but I could never really connect with L.A. It was too – I don’t even know how to describe it, because it was some good people in L.A., but by – I think by 1960, Charles, Ornette, Cherry, Hig, all of them, they went to New York. Garnet Brown was out…

116.t: Dress Blues guests: Eric Dolphy and the TV directors
116.s: Musicians on Dress Blues, a jam with Dolphy, directors, Buddy Collette and Red Callender.
116.q: When I saw Gerald – I knew Gerald pretty good, because I met Gerald when I first went out there. I never did – the t.v. show that I was doing, Dress Blues, a lot of singers and some musicians did that show. It was one of those freebee things. I’m sure at one time something – Gerald played – he’s a…

451.t: The lavender Cadillac drive to Los Angeles
451.s: The cross-country car delivery, Joe Dolny and Aunt Eva as reasons to go, practicing in the back seat, and visiting the Musicians Union.
451.q: Oh, that’s right. Yeah, I forgot that. Yeah, it was a lavender Cadillac. Lavender. And I had a friend in L.A. that I had studied big band arranging with. A guy named Joe Dolny, D-O-L-N-Y. And I knew that he could probably help me out there. And I had an Aunt Eva. I don’t know if we were technically…

451.t: Meeting Jimmy Giuffre and Red Mitchell at jam sessions
451.s: Meeting Giuffre outside a Hollywood Boulevard jam, their last phone calls, and Red Mitchell and an Ornette Coleman record date.
451.ch: Los Angeles: Chico Hamilton, Webster, Giuffre
451.q: Yeah, that was a bit later. I had gotten to know… Oh, there were some jam sessions in Los Angeles at, at a club… that’s where I met Jimmy Giuffre and Red Mitchell, and I got to know Red there. And I remember… (laughs) I remember meeting Jimmy Giuffre outside this club one time, and I really admired…

451.s: Hall recalls the Lighthouse, Shelly's Manne-Hole and other places in L.A.
451.ch: Los Angeles: Chico Hamilton, Webster, Giuffre
451.q: Let me see… They probably were, will, after you’ve gone to sleep tonight.

451.t: Long club residencies and the Les Paul guitar at The Strollers
451.s: Six nights a week for months in a barroom, the Soupy Sales broadcast, and switching to a Les Paul to cut through.
451.ch: Los Angeles: Chico Hamilton, Webster, Giuffre
451.q: In a, in a sense I guess I do. Yeah, I hadn’t thought of that too much. I’m sure there are jobs now where maybe they have the same piano player for a few months or something like that, but it was perfect, though, because we’re at this club called The Strollers. I assume it was six nights a week for…

451.s: The quintet's personnel, the long run at The Strollers in Long Beach, and what the job meant to him.
451.ch: Los Angeles: Chico Hamilton, Webster, Giuffre
451.q: Yeah, it was… Well, first of all, it literally was… I won’t say a lifesaver but I needed a job. (laughs) And I could, with my background I could, it would… Fred Katz played cello and piano. And then Buddy Collette played the woodwinds — clarinet and alto, and I don’t know if he played tenor. Carson…

451.t: Why L.A. rather than New York; music store and Stravinsky
451.s: New York frightened him; in L.A. he worked in a music store and attended classical concerts.
451.ch: Los Angeles: Chico Hamilton, Webster, Giuffre
451.q: Somehow it did because that’s, that was, that was where the serious jazzers were, I thought, then and still do in a way, I guess, but… Yeah, that, that’s interesting. And as you know, I had it first, when I first came here, I got a sublet right down the block. It had been Dick Katz’s apartment. Oh,…

367.t: After Detroit: Dayton, then California and Les Hite
367.s: Wilson went to his Dandridge-sister wife in California; Young stayed in Dayton, tried Lee and Lester Young's band, then joined Les Hite with Wilson's help.
367.q: 1942. When I went on home to Dayton, Gerald went…Gerald went to California. Now that‘s when Gerald went to California, because he was married to one of the Dandridge sisters. And they were from California. Gerald was married to Vivian I think her name was Vivian.

367.t: Family, moving to Long Island and then to California
367.s: Young explains his wife and family were in Dayton, he later moved them to Bayside, Long Island, and moved west when the Tonight Show did.
367.q: For some reason I didn‘t, I went back to Dayton, my wife, my family…

367.t: Leaving New York for California and liking it
367.s: Young says leaving the Thad-Mel band was the hard part of leaving New York and he has always liked California's weather and people.
367.q: [laughs] Well… boy. But that was a good band. Thad and Mel formed that band and they asked me, ―Snooky would you come play with this band?‖ and I said, ―Sure Thad, you know I‘m going to play with that band.‖ And when I had to leave New York and leave the band Thad and I, we just was almost in tears…

367.t: The Tonight Show moves to Hollywood
367.s: Young was happy to follow the show to California, with Doc Severinsen as leader and many friends there.
367.q: Well I‘ll tell you, it was kind of a strange feeling, and I felt that it, I kind of felt that, you can‘t leave New York without feeling something, you know what I‘m saying, but it worked out for me. It worked out for me because I loved California. And then, I had a lot of friends out here. And Doc…

367.t: Tape change; California weather versus Florida and Ohio
367.s: After a tape change Young compares Florida and Ohio humidity with California and says why he loves California.
367.q: …bands and things, and this was the state, I was down in Florida I was every place. I don‘t care for Florida, the weather and things, I like California. I don‘t mean anything about… I‘m talking about the weather and everything that‘s what I really meant when I said I didn‘t care for, I really…

367.t: Carson wanted the band to swing more
367.s: Young says the band became more jazz-oriented, especially after the move to California, because Carson and Doc wanted jazz players.
367.q: Ed Shaughnessy, Grady Tate, it was another drummer, he didn‘t stay there though that did the show in New York, NBC I‘m talking about, but Ed Shaughnessy and Grady Tate turned out to, but there was another guy who was on there, but he didn‘t stay, I don‘t know why. But, when Grady Tate came on…

238.t: Arriving in Los Angeles: relatives, Clarence Hart and the Dunbar Hotel
238.s: Her aunts and cousins were in California and Clarence Hart had moved there to work in painting and decorating; her first job was at the Dunbar Hotel.
238.q: Well, I'm glad of that too. I'm glad of that too. But you know, of course I suppose I had the same experience that Nat King Cole had, and there are a few other musicians too that has had the same experience. When I went to work, for instance my very first job here was at the

238.t: Coming to Los Angeles in 1935 to her aunt Lucille Avery
238.s: She lived with her aunt near Central Avenue and cousin Irving Jordan introduced her around.
238.q: Lucille. Her name was Lucille Avery. And she lived just a block from Central Avenue, on the east side. And my cousin, one of my cousins, knew everybody on the avenue, because they lived in that neighborhood, they'd been living there for many years because my aunt had been out here for a number of…

238.t: Club Alabam, Rochester and Lillian Randolph
238.s: Everyone went to Central Avenue's Club Alabam; she remembers Eddie Anderson's mop act with Johnnie Taylor and her friend Lillian Randolph.
238.q: Dunbar Hotel, and at the club. At that time the Club Alabam. I don't know how I got into the Club Alabam. I didn't talk about that, oh my gracious me, well that was something. The thing that was so exciting, Pat, when I first came here, was the fact that everybody, anybody who was anybody went to…

238.t: Clubs on and around Central Avenue
238.s: She and Willard sort out the Cotton Club, Bell Tavern, Apex, Club Alabam and Curtis Mosby's role.
238.q: Then on Central Avenue, my gracious me, every little place, every little bar on Central Avenue or anywhere, had entertainment, some type of entertainment. It was just marvelous.

238.t: Shep's Playhouse, Bronzeville and Shep Kelly's place
238.s: She and Willard discuss the wartime Bronzeville area and Shep's Playhouse, and she recalls a year as a single at Shep Kelly's on Ivar.
238.ch: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
238.q: That's unfortunate, because it -- it's a smart room, too. It's a very smart room, you know. You know, that comes to mind too, another room that I worked that I loved, and it was a room called Shep's --

238.t: Lena Horne, Curran's Merry-Go-Round and Vine Street radio row
238.s: The group played intermissions with Lena Horne at the Little Troc and at Curran's Merry-Go-Round, with Willard and Nellie placing the Radio Room on Vine Street.
238.ch: Four Chocolate Drops, San Diego and Club Royal
238.q: Well, we worked with Lena. We worked with Lena Horne, when they first brought her out here. Her first nightclub engagement, I think, was at the Little Troc out on Sunset Boulevard. I worked -- well, this group was of course just an intermission group, you know. But I worked with Lena, and then…

51.t: Why Ory chose California over Chicago
51.s: Ory says he was meant to join Oliver in Chicago but heard of the good climate and stayed in Los Angeles.
51.q: No, first I was supposed to meet Joe in Chicago and join him, you know. Yeah. They'll get back together. And I heard about this good climate out here, you see. And I changed my mind and I came to Los Angeles. And when I was here, Joe, I told him I didn't know whether I was going to stay or not, so…

455.t: Leaving Hines and returning to New York
455.s: After a second California tour in 1941, Budd quits Hines in December 1942, goes through Dallas and joins his second wife Bernice in New York.
455.q: And later on when I was in Honolulu with Benny Goodman, well he had a television show, him and his wife. But any way, '41 we went back to California, and this time we went out there and we made some V disk -- no, I mean that's with Billy Eckstein -- I mean with Earl Hines. We went back to…

13.t: Celebrities and Sunday night at the Grand Terrace
13.s: Movie stars visited; Sunday was party night.
13.q: : Yeah, like Leon Parr, George Raft, oh, the stars, you know, that was stars back in them days. All of them, when they come to Chicago, they'd come by the Grand Terrace.
